33330: Executes his father's killers, spares their sons
33331: He executes the servants who assassinated Joash but not their children, obeying the law that each person dies for his own sin (Deut 24:16).
33332: Victory over Edom; worships its gods
33333: He kills ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, then brings home Edom's gods and worships them, rejecting a prophet's rebuke.
33335: Proud after Edom, he challenges Israel. Jehoash replies with a fable of a thistle and a cedar, then defeats him at Beth-shemesh, breaks down Jerusalem's wall and loots the temple.
33337: A conspiracy forms in Jerusalem; he flees to Lachish and is killed there.
33338: Amaziah, son of Joash, reigned over Judah for twenty-nine years (about 796 to 767 BC, overlapping with his son Uzziah's co-regency). The verdict of the text is that he did what was right, 'yet not like David', and Chronicles adds 'not with a whole heart'. He began justly and defeated Edom, but then worshipped Edom's captured gods and foolishly provoked Israel, which humiliated him and plundered Jerusalem. Like his father, he died by assassination.
33339: Reigned twenty-nine years; did right but not like David; high places remained (2 Kgs 14:1-4). Spared the killers' children (2 Kgs 14:6). Defeated Edom (2 Kgs 14:7). Defeated by Jehoash (2 Kgs 14:11-14). Killed at Lachish (2 Kgs 14:19). Chronicles: hired and then dismissed Israelite mercenaries (2 Chr 25:6-10), worshipped Edom's gods (2 Chr 25:14), rejected the prophet (2 Chr 25:15-16).
33340: Ambitious and touchy; quick to take credit, slow to take advice.
33345: Thiele, end of his effective rule; lived to about 732
33348: When his father Uzziah is struck with leprosy, Jotham governs the palace and judges the people.
33349: Builds the Upper Gate and forts
33350: He builds the upper gate of the temple, works on the wall of Ophel, and builds cities and towers in Judah's hills and forests.
33352: He defeats the Ammonites and receives tribute for three years.
33353: Jotham, son of Uzziah, ruled Judah as regent while his father was a leper and then as king, about 750 to 735 BC by Thiele's reckoning (the overlap with Ahaz is debated). The verdict of the text is that he did what was right, as his father had, though the people still acted corruptly and the high places remained. Chronicles says he 'became mighty because he ordered his ways before the LORD'. He was a builder and successful in war. Isaiah, Hosea and Micah were active in his days.
33354: Governed for Uzziah (2 Kgs 15:5). Reigned sixteen years; did right like Uzziah; high places remained (2 Kgs 15:32-35). Did not enter the temple as his father had (2 Chr 27:2). Became mighty because he ordered his ways before the LORD (2 Chr 27:6). Named in Isa 1:1, Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1, and in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:9).
33355: 2 Kgs 15:30 mentions a 'twentieth year of Jotham', more than his sixteen-year reign. Thiele explains this by counting from the start of his co-regency and supposing Ahaz took effective control while Jotham was still alive; others suspect a scribal or editorial issue (debated).
33356: Steady, quiet and methodical; a builder who prefers careful work to grand speeches.
33362: As a sheep breeder-king he pays Israel a heavy tribute in lambs and wool.
33364: When Ahab dies he refuses to pay.
33365: Sacrifices his son on the wall
33366: Beaten back and besieged at Kir-hareseth by Israel, Judah and Edom, he offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall. 'Great wrath' comes upon Israel and the allies withdraw.
33367: Mesha was king of Moab, east of the Dead Sea, in the ninth century BC. He paid Israel heavy tribute in sheep and wool until Ahab died, then rebelled. When a coalition of Israel, Judah and Edom besieged him, he sacrificed his heir on the city wall, and the attackers withdrew. Mesha's own account survives on the Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone, about 840 BC), which credits his god Chemosh with freeing Moab from Omri's house and mentions Israel and very probably the LORD (YHWH) by name.
33368: A sheep breeder who paid Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams (2 Kgs 3:4). Rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 3:5). Sacrificed his eldest son; great wrath came on Israel and they withdrew (2 Kgs 3:27).
33370: Readers differ on whose wrath this is: God's anger at Israel, the fury of Moab spurred by the sacrifice, the allies' horror, or (in some critical readings) the power of Chemosh as the original story imagined it (debated).
33371: The Mesha Stele, found in 1868, confirms Mesha, Omri, and Israel's domination of Moab; its account of how and when Moab broke free differs from 2 Kings 3 in emphasis and perhaps timing (scholarly-consensus on the stele's authenticity; details debated).
33372: Proud and pious toward his own god; boasts in the style of an ancient victory inscription.
33379: Made king by the people of the land
33380: After Josiah was killed at Megiddo, "the people of the land" (the landowning citizens of Judah) anointed Josiah's son Jehoahaz king, passing over his older brother Eliakim. He was 23 and reigned three months.
33382: Neco put him in chains at Riblah in Syria, fined Judah heavily, set his brother Eliakim (renamed Jehoiakim) on the throne, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.
33384: Jeremiah tells the people not to weep for the dead Josiah but for the one who has gone away, Shallum, because he will never return to see his homeland.
33385: Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, was a son of Josiah who became king of Judah in 609 BC after his father died fighting Pharaoh Neco. He lasted only three months. Neco removed him, took him as a prisoner to Egypt, and replaced him with his brother Jehoiakim, who would pay Egypt tribute. Jehoahaz never came home.
33386: He was 23 when he began to reign and reigned three months; his mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (2 Kgs 23:31). Kings says he did evil like his fathers (2 Kgs 23:32). Jeremiah calls him Shallum and says he will die where he was taken captive (Jer 22:11-12). 1 Chronicles lists Shallum among Josiah's sons (1 Chr 3:15).
33387: The choice of the younger son by "the people of the land" is often read as a vote for Josiah's anti-Egyptian policy; Neco's swift removal of him fits Egypt's attempt to control the Levant after 609 BC (debated, but widely held).
33389: Many read Ezekiel's lament over a young lion taken in hooks to Egypt as a picture of Jehoahaz (Ezek 19:1-4).
33390: The Babylonian Chronicle records that in 609 BC Egypt marched north to help the last Assyrian forces at Harran. Josiah died trying to stop that march, and Neco then treated Judah as an Egyptian vassal (scholarly-consensus).
33391: He is the first king of Judah to die in exile, an early sign of the deportations that followed.
33392: Young and uncertain, speaking with the borrowed confidence of a man pushed forward by others, then with the flat grief of a prisoner far from home.
33396: Death early in 597 BC, depending on how the last months are counted
33398: Vassal of Egypt, then of Babylon
33400: Neco made Eliakim king in place of his brother Jehoahaz and renamed him Jehoiakim. He taxed the land to pay Egypt's tribute. He was 25 and reigned eleven years.
33401: Builds a palace with unpaid labour
33402: Jeremiah condemns him for building a grand house with cedar panelling while not paying his workers, and contrasts him with his father Josiah, who did justice. He predicts Jehoiakim will have "the burial of an ass", dragged out and thrown beyond the gates.
33404: When Uriah son of Shemaiah prophesied as Jeremiah did, the king sought to kill him, had him brought back from Egypt, and struck him down with the sword.
33406: In winter, as the scroll of Jeremiah's words was read to him, he cut off each few columns with a knife and threw them into the fire. Jeremiah dictated the scroll again to Baruch with more added.
33408: He served Nebuchadnezzar three years, then rebelled. Raiding bands from Babylon, Aram, Moab and Ammon came against Judah. Kings says he "slept with his fathers"; Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him to take him to Babylon.
33409: Jehoiakim, a son of Josiah, ruled Judah from 609 to about 598 BC. Egypt put him on the throne, but after Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC he had to serve Nebuchadnezzar. He is remembered mainly as Jeremiah's great opponent: he killed the prophet Uriah, burned Jeremiah's scroll, and later rebelled against Babylon, which brought the first great siege of Jerusalem.
33410: He did evil in the sight of the LORD (2 Kgs 23:37; 2 Chr 36:5). His mother was Zebidah, daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah (2 Kgs 23:36). Jeremiah says none would lament him (Jer 22:18) and that none of his line would sit on David's throne (Jer 36:30). His death is described differently: Kings says he slept with his fathers (2 Kgs 24:6), Chronicles says he was bound in bronze chains to be taken to Babylon (2 Chr 36:6), and Jeremiah predicts a dishonoured corpse (Jer 22:19; Jer 36:30).
33411: Some suggest he was bound for deportation but released or died before leaving, and that his body was later treated with dishonour, so all three accounts can stand together.
33412: Others think the sources reflect different traditions, and that Jeremiah's oracle was a prophetic curse whose literal fulfilment is not recorded. This remains debated.
33413: Rabbinic tradition portrays him as one of the most wicked kings, guilty of grave sins beyond those named in Scripture.
33414: The Babylonian Chronicle confirms the main events around him: Nebuchadnezzar's victory over Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC (cf. Jer 46:2), his campaigns in the west, and a costly battle with Egypt in 601 BC that likely encouraged Judah's rebellion (scholarly-consensus). The same chronicle records Jerusalem's capture in March 597 BC, just after Jehoiakim's death.
33415: His burning of the scroll became a classic picture of a ruler trying to silence God's word, and of the word surviving anyway.
33416: Cold, proud and dismissive, a man who talks over the reading and treats a prophet's warning as so much kindling.
33422: If he was eight at accession (2 Chr 36:9 in the Hebrew)
33425: After a reign of three months he went out to the Babylonian king with his mother, servants and officials and gave himself up.
33426: Deported with the first great exile
33427: He was taken to Babylon with the royal family, officials, craftsmen and soldiers, among them the young priest Ezekiel. Temple treasures were carried off too.
33429: Jeremiah says that even if Coniah were the signet ring on God's hand, he would be pulled off, and that no descendant of his would prosper on David's throne.
33431: In the 37th year of his exile the new king of Babylon freed him, spoke kindly to him, gave him a seat above the other captive kings, and provided him a daily allowance for the rest of his life.
33432: Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah or Coniah, was the son of Jehoiakim. He became king at about 18, reigned three months, and surrendered Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar in March 597 BC. He spent the rest of his life in Babylon. The books of Kings end with his release from prison about 37 years later, a small sign of hope that David's line had not ended. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus runs through him.
33433: He was 18 when he began to reign (2 Kgs 24:8); the Hebrew of 2 Chr 36:9 says eight, which most scholars treat as a copying slip. His mother was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan (2 Kgs 24:8). 1 Chronicles lists his sons, including Shealtiel and Pedaiah, and through them Zerubbabel (1 Chr 3:17-19). Matthew names him Jechonias in Jesus' line (Matt 1:11-12). Ezekiel dates his visions by the years of "King Jehoiachin's exile" (Ezek 1:2).
33434: Some rabbinic texts hold that Jehoiachin repented in prison and that the curse of Jer 22:30 was lifted, which is why his grandson Zerubbabel could lead the return (Hag 2:23 reverses the signet-ring image).
33435: Christian readers have long discussed how Jesus can be heir of David through Jeconiah given the curse. Common answers: the curse applied to his own lifetime or was lifted; Jesus inherits the legal right through Joseph without being a biological descendant; or Luke's different genealogy traces another line. This is debated.
33436: The release at the end of Kings is read by many as a deliberately muted note of hope for the Davidic house written during the exile.
33437: Extra-biblical evidence for Jehoiachin is unusually strong. The Babylonian Chronicle says that on the 2nd of Adar in Nebuchadnezzar's 7th year (16 March 597 BC) he captured "the city of Judah", seized its king and appointed a king of his own choice (scholarly-consensus). Clay ration tablets found in Babylon's royal palace and published by E. F. Weidner in 1939 list oil rations for "Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahud" and his five sons; one tablet is dated to Nebuchadnezzar's 13th year, about 592 BC (scholarly-consensus).
33438: He became the reference point for Judah's exiles. Ezekiel counted time by his captivity, and his descendants Shealtiel and Zerubbabel carried the royal line into the return.
33439: Subdued and courteous, the manner of a young king who learned early to bow, speaking with the patience of a man who waited decades for a kind word.
33444: Murder some years later, possibly linked to the deportation of 582 BC (Jer 52:30)
33449: After Jerusalem fell, Nebuchadnezzar set Gedaliah over the poor people left in the land. He urged the scattered Judeans to serve Babylon, settle down and gather the harvest, and many returned.
33451: The Babylonians brought Jeremiah out of the guard court and committed him to Gedaliah. Jeremiah chose to stay with him at Mizpah.
33452: Ignores the warning and is murdered
33453: Johanan son of Kareah warned him that Ishmael son of Nethaniah, of royal descent, had been sent by the king of Ammon to kill him. Gedaliah refused to believe it. In the seventh month Ishmael killed him at a meal, along with Judeans and Babylonian soldiers.
33454: Gedaliah came from a family of royal officials who had backed Jeremiah: his grandfather Shaphan served Josiah, and his father Ahikam protected Jeremiah from a lynch mob. After Jerusalem fell in 586 BC the Babylonians made him governor of what was left of Judah, based at Mizpah. He tried to rebuild ordinary life, but a member of the royal family murdered him. His death drove the survivors to flee to Egypt in fear of Babylon.
33455: He is "Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan" (2 Kgs 25:22; Jer 39:14). His father Ahikam (not a separate profile here) protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24). He swore to the people that serving Babylon would go well with them (Jer 40:9). He was killed by Ishmael in the seventh month (Jer 41:1-2), and the survivors went to Egypt against Jeremiah's advice (Jer 41:16-43:7).
33456: The Fast of Gedaliah on the 3rd of Tishri mourns his murder as the end of Jewish self-rule after the destruction. Many link it to the "fast of the seventh month" in Zech 7:5 and Zech 8:19 (tradition).
33458: He is often seen as a decent man undone by trust; his refusal to suspect Ishmael is read either as nobility or as fatal naivety.
33459: A clay seal impression from Lachish reads "belonging to Gedaliah, who is over the house", the title of a royal steward. Some scholars identify this with Gedaliah son of Ahikam before he became governor; others think it is another man. The identification is debated. The year of his murder is not stated: many place it in 586 BC, soon after the city fell, while others link it with a further deportation in 582 BC (Jer 52:30).
33460: His murder closed the last chance for a Judean community in the land under Babylon, and it is still remembered by a Jewish fast day.
33461: Calm, practical and reassuring, a steady administrator who speaks of harvests and settling down, and who would rather trust than suspect.
33462: The Fast of Gedaliah (Tzom Gedaliah) is kept on the day after Rosh Hashanah to mourn his assassination.
33470: Pulls Jeremiah out of the cistern
33471: When officials threw Jeremiah into a muddy cistern to die, Ebed-melech went to King Zedekiah and protested. With thirty men he lowered rags and ropes, told Jeremiah to pad his armpits, and drew him up.
33473: God sent word through Jeremiah that when the city fell Ebed-melech would not be handed over to the men he feared, "because you have put your trust in me".
33474: Ebed-melech was a Cushite (from the region south of Egypt) serving in King Zedekiah's palace. When Jeremiah was left to die in a muddy cistern, he spoke up to the king and organised the rescue, even thinking to send rags so the ropes would not cut. God promised him safety when Jerusalem fell.
33475: He is called a Cushite and a saris, a word that can mean eunuch or simply court official (Jer 38:7). He was rewarded for trusting God (Jer 39:18).
33476: Often set beside the Ethiopian official of Acts 8 as an African outsider who showed faith while insiders failed.
33477: Some rabbinic and later legends identify him with other figures or say he entered paradise alive (tradition, late sources).
33478: Direct and brave, speaking plainly to a king in public, with a practical kindness that thinks of small details.
33481: Fourth year of Zedekiah reckoned as 593 BC
33482: If the fourth year is 593 BC
33485: Predicts Babylon's fall within two years
33486: In the temple, before priests and people, he announced that God had broken the yoke of Babylon and that within two years the temple vessels, King Jeconiah and the exiles would return.
33488: Jeremiah answered that he wished it were so, but that a prophet of peace is proved only when his word comes true. Hananiah took the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck and broke it as a sign.
33490: Jeremiah returned with the word that wooden yokes would be replaced by iron ones, told Hananiah that God had not sent him and that he would die that year. He died in the seventh month.
33491: Hananiah was a prophet from Gibeon who publicly contradicted Jeremiah in the temple. He promised that Babylon's power would be broken within two years and the exiles brought home. He broke the wooden yoke Jeremiah wore as a sign of submission to Babylon. Jeremiah said God had not sent him, and he died within months.
33492: He spoke in the LORD's name using the same formula as true prophets (Jer 28:2). Jeremiah accused him of making the people trust in a lie and of preaching rebellion against the LORD (Jer 28:15-16). He died the same year (Jer 28:17).
33494: The episode is a test case for discerning true and false prophecy: both men claim God's authority, and the outcome follows Deuteronomy's test of fulfilment (Deut 18:21-22).
33495: Many see Hananiah as sincerely patriotic, drawing on older Zion traditions of God's protection of Jerusalem, rather than a cynical liar.
33496: Confident and rousing, a crowd-pleaser who uses all the right prophetic phrases and promises good news on a short timetable.
33501: Beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks
33502: Hearing Jeremiah prophesy disaster, Pashhur, chief officer in the LORD's house, struck him and put him in the stocks at the upper Benjamin Gate overnight.
33504: When released, Jeremiah told him God had renamed him Magor-missabib, "terror on every side", and that he and his household would go captive to Babylon and die there.
33505: Pashhur son of Immer was a priest in charge of order in the Jerusalem temple. He had Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks for preaching judgment. Jeremiah gave him a new name, "Terror on every side", and said he would die in Babylon. Another Pashhur, son of Malchiah, later urged that Jeremiah be put to death (Jer 21:1; Jer 38:1-6).
33506: He is a priest and chief officer of the temple (Jer 20:1) who had also prophesied falsely to his friends (Jer 20:6). Scripture names at least two Pashhurs in Jeremiah's time; this profile is the son of Immer.
33507: A clay seal impression found in Jerusalem reads "Gedaliah son of Pashhur", matching the name of an official in Jer 38:1. Whether that Pashhur is this man, Pashhur son of Malchiah, or someone else is not known (speculative).
33508: Officious and authoritarian, a temple manager who treats a troublesome prophet as a matter for discipline.
33513: Head of a family of officials
33515: Sent to the temple to pay the workers
33516: In Josiah's 18th year the king sent Shaphan to the high priest Hilkiah to release the collected money to the workmen repairing the temple.
33517: Reads the book of the law to the king
33518: Hilkiah handed him the book of the law found in the temple. Shaphan read it and then read it aloud to Josiah, who tore his clothes.
33520: With Hilkiah, his son Ahikam and others, he went to ask Huldah what God was saying through the book.
33521: Shaphan was the royal secretary of King Josiah. He brought the book of the law found in the temple to the king and read it aloud, which set off Josiah's great reform. His family remained influential for a generation. His son Ahikam saved Jeremiah's life, another son Gemariah let Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll from his room, and his grandson Gedaliah became governor of Judah after Jerusalem fell.
33522: His sons named in Scripture include Ahikam (2 Kgs 22:12; Jer 26:24), Gemariah (Jer 36:10-12) and Elasah, who carried Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jer 29:3). A Jaazaniah son of Shaphan appears in Ezekiel's vision of idol worship (Ezek 8:11), probably a different Shaphan. Gedaliah is his grandson through Ahikam (2 Kgs 25:22).
33523: Many scholars think Shaphan's family were a key circle of scribes behind the Deuteronomic reform and perhaps behind the preserving of Jeremiah's words (debated).
33524: A clay seal impression found in the City of David in 1982 reads "belonging to Gemaryahu son of Shaphan". Many identify him with Gemariah son of Shaphan of Jer 36, though the name pair could belong to another man (debated).
33525: Shaphan's household shows how faithful officials could shelter God's messengers inside a hostile court for decades.
33526: Careful and businesslike, a civil servant who reports facts first, then quietly reads the document that changes everything.
33532: Finder of the book of the law
33533: Finds the book of the law
33534: During temple repairs Hilkiah found "the book of the law" (Chronicles: "given by Moses") and gave it to Shaphan the secretary.
33536: Josiah sent Hilkiah and others to ask God about the book; they went to the prophetess Huldah, who confirmed judgment but promised Josiah peace.
33538: At Josiah's command he and the priests removed the objects made for Baal, Asherah and the stars, and burned them outside Jerusalem.
33540: As a chief officer of God's house he gave thousands of animals to the priests for Josiah's Passover.
33541: Hilkiah was high priest in the reign of Josiah. While the temple was being repaired in 622 BC he found a scroll called "the book of the law". Its warnings shook the king and led to the most thorough religious reform in Judah's history, including the removal of idols from the temple and a national Passover.
